title: Muscat
description: Also called Moscato, Moscatel and Muskateller. The family of grapes that actually taste of grapes.
L: The grape that tastes of grapes
Explain why it smells of grapes

Muscat is one of the few wine grapes whose wine smells of fresh grapes. Add orange blossom, rose, elderflower, peach and orange peel. Muscat wines can be dry, sweet, sparkling or fortified, from light Moscato d'Asti to rich Rutherglen Muscat. It's one of the oldest known grape families.

Muscat's aroma comes from high levels of terpenes, especially linalool, floral and citrus, and geraniol, rose. These compounds are present in the grape itself, which is why the wine smells like eating the fruit. Many Muscats are also table grapes and raisins.
Which compounds give Muscat its grapey, floral aroma?
Terpenes, abundant in Muscat, give floral and grape aromas.

If a wine smells exactly like fresh grapes, with orange blossom, it's almost certainly Muscat. Dry Muscat is a surprise: aromatic like a sweet wine, but dry on the palate. Compared with Gewürztraminer, Muscat is more grapey and floral, less lychee and spice.
Not true. Muscat is made dry, for example in Alsace, as well as sweet and fortified.

It's made dry, sweet, sparkling and fortified

Muscat is a family of over 200 grapes. The finest is Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, small-berried, used in Asti, Alsace, Beaumes-de-Venise and Rutherglen. Muscat of Alexandria, larger-berried and less refined, grows in Spain, Portugal's Setúbal, Sicily as Zibibbo, and Chile. Muscat Ottonel, lighter, grows in Alsace and Austria. Some Muscats are pink or black.

Muscat is among the oldest grapes, probably from Greece or the eastern Mediterranean; the Greeks and Romans spread it. Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains is thought to be the oldest; Muscat of Alexandria is its offspring with a table grape. It grows in Greece, as Moschato on Samos, and across the Mediterranean.
Match each Muscat to its region.
The Muscat family spreads around the Mediterranean.
Zibibbo, Sicily's name for Muscat of Alexandria, makes the famous Passito di Pantelleria from sun-dried grapes on a volcanic island south of Sicily.
Which Muscat is considered the finest?
Its small berries give the most refined wines.
Muscat is a family of over 200 grapes
Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains is the finest
It spread from Greece across the Mediterranean

In Piedmont, Moscato Bianco makes Moscato d'Asti, lightly sparkling, frizzante, sweet and about 5.5% alcohol, and Asti, fully sparkling, around 7%. Fermentation in a pressure tank is stopped by chilling, leaving sugar and trapped bubbles. They smell of peach, grape and orange blossom.

Alsace makes dry Muscat, intensely aromatic yet dry, a classic aperitif. Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and Muscat de Rivesaltes, in southern France, are fortified, sweet vins doux naturels. Samos, in Greece, makes sweet Muscats, some from sun-dried grapes. Austria makes dry Muskateller.
Match each wine to its style.

Since the 2000s, Moscato has become hugely popular worldwide, especially in the US, where sweet, light, fruity Moscatos from California and Australia are widely sold. They're often made in Asti's style but from Muscat of Alexandria or other varieties.
Moscato d'Asti usually has about ____% alcohol.
Low alcohol and sweetness come from stopping fermentation early.
Moscato d'Asti is sweet, frizzante and about 5.5%
Alsace makes dry Muscat; southern France fortified sweet Muscat
Moscato has become a global trend
Explain how ageing changes fortified Muscat

Rutherglen, in north-east Victoria, Australia, makes some of the world's richest fortified wines from a dark-skinned Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, called Brown Muscat. Grapes are picked very ripe, fortified, and aged for years in old casks in hot sheds, often in solera-like systems. The wines are dark, syrupy, with raisin, toffee, coffee and orange peel.

Rutherglen Muscat has four levels: Rutherglen, Classic, Grand and Rare, each older and more concentrated. In Portugal, Moscatel de Setúbal, from Muscat of Alexandria near Lisbon, is fortified and macerated on skins for months, giving orange peel, apricot and honey. Aged versions reach 20 years or more.
Order Rutherglen Muscat's levels from youngest to oldest.
Each level is older and more concentrated.

As fortified Muscat ages in cask, it oxidises slowly and concentrates through evaporation. Fresh grape and orange blossom turn into raisin, fig, toffee, coffee and rancio, a nutty, complex character. Old Rare Rutherglen blends can include wines decades old.
Rutherglen Muscat is dark, syrupy and long-aged
It has four levels: Rutherglen, Classic, Grand, Rare
Moscatel de Setúbal is Portugal's fortified Muscat
Pair each Muscat style with food
Know how long to keep them

Dry Muscat suits asparagus, a classic in Alsace, and aperitifs. Moscato d'Asti suits fruit salads, panettone and light desserts, even brunch. Beaumes-de-Venise suits fruit tarts and melon. Rutherglen Muscat suits sticky toffee pudding, chocolate, coffee desserts and blue cheese.

Serve Moscato d'Asti and dry Muscat at 6 to 8 degrees, sweet fortified Muscat at 12 to 16. Moscato d'Asti and dry Muscat are best within a year or two; their aroma fades. Fortified Muscats, already aged, keep for weeks once opened.
Its toffee and raisin notes match rich desserts.
Dry Alsace Muscat with white asparagus in spring is one of the few successful asparagus pairings.
Moscato d'Asti is best drunk young.
Yes. Its fresh grape aroma is its charm, and it fades with time.
Dry Muscat suits asparagus; Moscato suits fruit desserts
Rutherglen Muscat suits toffee and chocolate
Drink Moscato young; fortified Muscat keeps
